title: The Song of the Sea and the Bitter Water
summary: On the far shore Moses and Israel sing a victory hymn to the LORD, who has thrown horse and rider into the sea and will lead his redeemed people to his holy dwelling; Miriam and the women answer with tambourines and dancing. Three days into the desert the people find only bitter water at Marah and grumble, and the LORD makes the water sweet, gives them a statute, and calls himself the LORD who heals. They come to the oasis of Elim.
story: Chapter 14 told the crossing of the sea in prose; chapter 15 answers it in song. This is the first hymn in the Bible, and it does more than look back. It moves from the sea to the future, imagining the nations trembling and Israel planted on God's mountain, and it ends by confessing the LORD as king forever. Then, abruptly, the story turns to the desert. Within three days the people who sang are grumbling about water. The chapter holds both sides of the wilderness years together: the glory of God's rescue and the fragility of the people's trust. Marah begins a series of testing stories (manna in chapter 16, water from the rock in chapter 17) in which God trains a freed people to depend on him before he gives them his law at Sinai.
historical:
The song describes the crossing of chapter 14, whose date and location are debated (see the notes there). The poem itself has drawn attention for its language. Many scholars, including Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman, have argued on grounds of grammar, vocabulary, and poetic form that it is among the oldest poems in the Hebrew Bible; others date it later, noting that verse 17 seems to envision a sanctuary already established, which some read as the temple in Jerusalem and others as the land of Canaan as God's dwelling. The peoples named in verses 14-15 (Philistia, Edom, Moab, and Canaan) are the nations Israel would meet on the road to the land.

The Desert of Shur lay in the northwest of the Sinai Peninsula, east of Egypt's border; Hagar fled toward it in Genesis 16:7. Marah and Elim have not been identified with certainty. Bitter or brackish springs are common in the region, and oases with palms and several springs also exist, so the narrative fits the terrain even if the exact sites are unknown.
cultural:
Victory songs were a known form in the ancient world, and in Israel women often led the celebration with hand drums and dancing, as when Jephthah's daughter came out to meet him (Judges 11:34) or when the women sang of Saul and David (1 Samuel 18:6-7). Miriam's refrain, sung back to the people, fits that pattern of call and response. She is called a prophetess, the first woman given that title in the Bible, which shows that she held a recognized role of leadership alongside her brothers (compare Micah 6:4).

The song borrows images its first hearers knew from the religious world around them and turns them to new use. Neighboring peoples told of storm gods who fought the sea and built a palace on a mountain after their victory. The Song of the Sea tells of the LORD using the sea as a weapon, not fighting it as a rival, and ends with him establishing his own dwelling and reigning. The question “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?” is a claim that the gods of Egypt and Canaan are no match for him. At Marah, the promise that God will not bring “the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians” recalls the plagues and presents the LORD as the one who holds both judgment and healing.
literary: Verses 1-18 are Hebrew poetry, built from parallel lines in which the second line echoes, sharpens, or completes the first: “Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power; Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy.” The song falls into two main parts. Verses 1-12 look back at the sea, with three images for the enemy's fall (sinking “like a stone”, consumed “like stubble”, sinking “like lead”). Verses 13-18 look forward to God leading his people to his holy place. The enemy's boast in verse 9 is a burst of six short clauses, each centered on the enemy himself (I will pursue, I will overtake, my hand will destroy), answered by a single line: God simply breathed. A prose summary (verse 19) and Miriam's refrain (verses 20-21) close the hymn, and a brief narrative (verses 22-27) returns to the road. The move from the song to the complaint at Marah is itself the point: praise can be sincere and still short-lived.

outline.t: The LORD has triumphed at the sea
The LORD will lead his people to his dwelling
Bitter water made sweet at Marah

doctrines.note: The song ends with the Bible's first explicit statement of God's kingship: “The LORD will reign forever and ever”. The victory at the sea is presented as the act of a king establishing his rule and his people.
The song praises God as incomparable, “majestic in holiness”, powerful in judgment, and full of loving devotion toward the people he has redeemed. Marah adds that he is the LORD who heals.

Israel's first response to salvation is worship in song, and Scripture's hymn book grows from here. At Marah, Moses models a different kind of prayer, crying out to God when the people only complain to Moses.

words.note: Gaal, to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer. The word belongs to family law: the nearest relative bought back land or freed a relative from debt or slavery (Leviticus 25:25, 47-49; Ruth 3-4). When the song speaks of “the people You have redeemed”, it pictures the LORD acting as Israel's next of kin.

Chesed, steadfast love or loyal love, rendered “loving devotion” in verse 13. It is love bound by commitment, the kind God shows within his covenant, and it becomes one of the central words for God's character in the Old Testament (34:6).

Yeshuah, salvation, deliverance. “He has become my salvation” (verse 2) names what the sea meant: rescue from a danger Israel could not escape. The same root lies behind the names Joshua and Jesus, both meaning something like the LORD saves.
Marah, meaning bitter. The place is named after its water. The same root lies behind the name Mara (bitter) that Naomi takes for herself in her grief (Ruth 1:20).

christ: Verse 2 is repeated almost word for word in Psalm 118:14 and Isaiah 12:2, so the song of the exodus became Israel's pattern for praising every later deliverance. Revelation takes it up at the end of the Bible, where those who have conquered the beast stand beside a sea and sing “the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3). That scene presents the final victory of Christ as a greater exodus and his people's praise as a greater version of this song. The chapter's confession that the LORD is the one who redeems, heals, and reigns is echoed in the Gospels' portrait of Jesus, who heals the sick and announces the kingdom of God. These links are drawn by the New Testament itself; the tree thrown into the water at Marah has often been read as a picture of the cross, but that is a later devotional reading, not something the text or the New Testament claims.

hard.q: What are we to make of praising God as “a warrior” and celebrating the drowning of an army?
hard.a: “The LORD is a warrior” (verse 3) can sound alien to modern readers. It helps to see what the song does and doesn't celebrate. Israel did not fight; the song gives the victory entirely to God, and it praises him for rescuing slaves from the army sent to recapture them. In the ancient world, calling a god a warrior meant he was able to protect and deliver his people; the song claims that power for the LORD alone. The Bible elsewhere shows restraint about rejoicing over the fall of enemies (Proverbs 24:17; Ezekiel 18:23), and later Jewish tradition preserved a story of God rebuking the angels who wished to sing while the Egyptians drowned. Readers differ on how to weigh the violence of such passages: some see it as just judgment on oppression, told in the idiom of the time; others emphasize that the Bible's own story moves toward a warrior who wins by suffering rather than by the sword (Revelation 5:5-6). Both recognize that the song's heart is not delight in death but gratitude for deliverance.

questions: Israel sang on the shore and grumbled three days later. What helps you keep remembering what God has done when a new hardship comes?
Miriam led the women in answering the song. Who in your life leads you into praise, and whom might you lead?
At Marah God called himself “the LORD who heals you.” What bitter places in your life do you need him to heal?
